beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime and never commit credentials to the repo; provide a .env.example with a placeholder instead.

Reuse a single MongoClient instance across the Node.js process, configure a connection pool (maxPoolSize) appropriate to concurrency, and set sensible timeouts (serverSelectionTimeoutMS and socketTimeoutMS) rather than opening/closing clients per request.
Use TLS/SSL for connections and restrict network access to the cluster (IP firewall, VNet, or private endpoints); do not send credentials over plaintext or expose the cluster publicly.

Create a compound unique index on (customerId, eventId) with unique:true to deduplicate events at write time; create the index idempotently at startup (createIndexes) or via setup script so repeated runs do not fail.

For high-throughput ingestion use unordered bulkWrite (ordered:false) and process BulkWriteError/writeErrors — treat duplicate-key errors (code 11000) as expected and continue without aborting the whole batch.

Limit bulkWrite batch sizes (e.g., 500–5000 documents depending on doc size and cluster limits) to avoid large memory usage, exceed per-request limits, or trigger large retries; tune batch size experimentally.
Make ingestion idempotent: include an application-level unique eventId and rely on the unique index for deduplication rather than trying to rely on retries to preserve idempotency.
Use upsert judiciously for dedup/write-if-not-exists scenarios (e.g., replaceOne with upsert:false when using unique index) instead of complex transactions if throughput is required.
Don't rely on multi-document transactions for high-throughput event ingestion—prefer single-document writes or bulk unordered writes and idempotent design to maximize throughput and reduce latency.

When using change streams, persist and periodically checkpoint resume tokens (or resumeAfter) so the consumer can resume after crashes; implement exponential backoff and reopen streams on transient errors.

Open change streams with an appropriate pipeline and maxAwaitTimeMS, and monitor for resumability errors; treat change-streams as long-lived cursors and guard against idle timeouts by handling resumable/non-resumable errors.

If the managed service exposes a platform-native change feed (e.g., Cosmos DB Change Feed), evaluate using that instead of MongoDB change streams if it offers better SLAs/availability or integrates better with Azure tooling.
Monitor and profile queries: capture slow operations, use explain() for queries to verify index usage (index intersection or covered queries), and add projections to return only necessary fields.
Use TTL indexes for ephemeral event data you only need for a bounded period (createIndex({eventTimestamp:1}, {expireAfterSeconds: N})) to bound storage growth for high-volume event streams.

For deployments with vector search enabled, store normalized float vectors in a fixed-dimension field and create the vector index with the cluster's supported index type (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) and correct dimension and metric; tune index parameters (efConstruction, M) and search ef/nearK for latency/recall tradeoffs.

When retrying write operations on transient errors, use idempotent retry semantics (exponential backoff, jitter) and ensure deduplication key (customerId + eventId) prevents duplicate logical events from being applied twice.

Provision throughput appropriately for sustained ingestion: either provision collection/database throughput or use autoscale if available; monitor RU consumption (or equivalent) and scale before throttling becomes frequent.

Avoid creating many large or wide compound indexes that include low-selectivity fields; design indexes to support actual query patterns (filter -> sort -> projection) and remove unused indexes during heavy ingestion to reduce write amplification.

Emit application metrics around bulkWrite throughput, bulk write error rates (duplicate-key counts), change-stream lag, and connection pool utilization; wire these to a monitoring system and alert on increased throttling or change-stream disconnects.

Make index creation and collection setup part of an idempotent bootstrap step (scripts or startup code) that checks for existing indexes/collections and only creates missing ones rather than failing if run multiple times.
Keep event documents small (avoid embedding large binary payloads) and store large payloads in object storage with a reference in the event document when size could approach document limits.
Handle partial bulk failures by examining BulkWriteResult and writeErrors: retry only the failed operations that are retryable (not duplicate-key) and do not blindly re-run entire batches.
Ensure proper IAM/role management: grant least privilege to the ingestion service (only insert/replace/find privileges on the target DB/collection) and rotate any long-lived keys regularly.

If change-stream tests time out, verify cluster-level support and permissions for change streams (MongoDB feature level, wire protocol version, and account roles) before assuming application bug; add diagnostic logging and short-lived test streams with immediate resume token capture.
